KHRONOFLARE

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

High-Level Project Summary

KhronoFlare turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire detections over Brazil into one consistent record and uses it to help civil-defense teams act before and during the fire season. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire differently: VIIRS detects about 4.5 times more hotspots, so joining the two records without correction makes recent years look worse than they were. We calibrate every satellite to a common reference, S-NPP VIIRS, harmonizing both hotspot counts and Fire Radiative Power, the latter by pairing MODIS and VIIRS pixels observed minutes apart. On this harmonized record we measure long-term trends, build a monthly fire calendar that shows how unusual each month is, and train a Random Forest that estimates, for each 0.5° area, the chance that next month will be critical compared with its own history (ROC-AUC ≈ 0.72 on independent tests). Two web tools put this to use: a Manager Outlook that ranks municipalities by expected risk for planning, and an Alert Console that ranks municipalities with active fires every three hours, requires a second approval and sends a standard CAP alert to a phone. The result is a reliable, comparable fire history and earlier, local warnings, built only on open NASA data and reusable in other countries.

Detailed Project Description

What it does and how it works

KhronoFlare turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections over Brazil into one consistent record and uses it to help civil-defense teams act before and during the fire season.

The problem: MODIS (Terra and Aqua, since 2000) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, since 2012) see fire differently. VIIRS has a 375 m pixel and detected about 4.5× more hotspots than MODIS over Brazil on the same day in our test. If the two records are joined without correction, every year after 2012 looks worse than it really was, and trends, anomalies and forecasts become misleading.

Our solution has four layers:

Hotspot-count harmonization. We apply the same filters to every sensor (nominal and high confidence, vegetation fires, clipped to Brazil’s border), use Standard Processing data before Near Real-Time, and convert every sensor to a common reference, S-NPP VIIRS. The conversion factors are estimated by region and calendar month, with a hierarchical fallback when data are sparse. They are chained across the satellite generations and checked with an out-of-sample test.

Fire Radiative Power (FRP) harmonization. Dividing totals is not enough, so we pair individual Aqua MODIS and VIIRS pixels observed within 5 minutes of each other. After cleaning duplicates and outliers, we calibrate MODIS FRP against VIIRS by viewing angle, with a separate term for night-time detections.

Trends and a fire calendar. We run robust statistical tests on the harmonized series (Sen’s slope, Mann-Kendall and Pettitt change-point) and build a monthly calendar showing, for each month, the historical median, the normal range and how unusual the current month is.

Next-month risk and alerts. A Random Forest on a 0.5° grid estimates the chance that next month will be critical for each area compared with that area’s own history. It reaches a ROC-AUC of about 0.72 on both time and space hold-outs. Two web tools use these results:

Manager Outlook: ranks cells and municipalities by expected risk for the coming month, so managers can plan brigades and campaigns.

Alert Console: ranks municipalities by active hotspots refreshed every 3 hours, helps draft an alert, requires approval by a second person, exports it in the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) format, and delivers a simulated alert to a real phone through a QR code.

Benefits

A fire record that is comparable from 2000 to today, so “more fire” means more fire and not a better sensor.

Earlier, local and relative warnings: the model flags months that will be abnormal for each specific place, not only the places that always burn.

A path from satellite data to a decision a manager can take, with checks that reduce false alarms.

Open code, tests and documented limitations, so other teams can reuse and verify the method.

Intended impact

Fire in Brazil threatens the Amazon, the Cerrado and the Pantanal, and smoke affects millions of people. We want municipal and state civil-defense teams, environmental agencies and researchers to plan the fire season with reliable long-term data, to target prevention where the coming month is likely to be unusually bad, and to warn people faster when fires are already burning. Because the method only depends on public NASA data, it can be applied to other countries.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Languages: Python 3.12, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML/CSS.

Data and modeling: pandas, NumPy, PyArrow/Parquet, SciPy, scikit-learn (Random Forest), Shapely, pyshp, Matplotlib.

Web: Leaflet with NASA GIBS imagery (VIIRS true color, Blue Marble, Black Marble), a vanilla-JS dashboard and an Angular app (standalone components, signals, English/Portuguese).

Infrastructure: GitHub with Git LFS, GitHub Actions (automatic 3-hour data refresh), Vercel for hosting, ntfy.sh for phone alerts, pytest for automated tests.

Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS C2, archive and NRT), NASA GIBS, IBGE boundaries and biomes, NOAA ONI and TNA climate indices.

Hardware: team members’ personal laptops and phones only; no special hardware.

Creative aspects

The name joins Khronos (time) and flare: the project is about making fire comparable across time.

We harmonize fire intensity pixel by pixel, not just hotspot counts, which goes beyond a single scaling factor.

Risk is measured against each place’s own normal, so the outlook shows both where fire is common and where this month is likely to be abnormal.

The alert flow brings practices from real emergency systems: a second person approves, the CAP standard is used, and an alert reaches a phone with a QR code during the demo.

Factors the team considered

Scientific validity: We validated out of sample instead of only fitting the data, and we dropped analyses that looked good but were circular, such as FRP versus brightness. We also tested climate indices and kept them as descriptive only because they did not improve the model.

Satellite changes: Terra and Aqua are drifting in orbit, so Aqua calibration stops in 2021 and the main trend uses 2003–2021. S-NPP stopped producing data in November 2026, so NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 take over as the reference.

Data limits, stated openly: NRT data cannot separate industrial heat sources from vegetation fires, a factor cannot create detections where MODIS saw none, and the model is weaker in the Cerrado and at predicting a worse-than-normal season.

Reliability: The FIRMS servers do not allow direct browser access (CORS), so a scheduled job prepares the data. A local relief map is kept as a backup because the GIBS imagery service sometimes fails under load.

Usability and accessibility: English by default with Portuguese on demand, high-contrast mode, adjustable font size, and a mobile layout.

Safety and ethics: The phone alert is a clearly labeled simulation on randomly named channels, no personal data is collected, and the code is open under the MIT License.
